claims.text: The initial HEA multilayers have coherent interfaces.
An ultrathin coherent tungsten interlayer will promote a transition from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
The proposed creep transition occurs from lower-temperature diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep at higher temperatures and stresses.
The tungsten interlayer forms coherent interfaces with adjacent HEA layers.
The tungsten interlayer reduces lattice mismatch.
The tungsten interlayer modifies the interfacial atomic structure.
Tungsten has a high melting point.
Tungsten has low atomic diffusivity.
Coherent incorporation of tungsten slows diffusion along HEA interfaces.
At increased stress or temperature, a coherent tungsten layer facilitates dislocation nucleation at interfaces.
At increased stress or temperature, a coherent tungsten layer facilitates dislocation transfer across interfaces.
Suppression of interfacial diffusion together with enhanced dislocation activity shifts the dominant creep mechanism toward dislocation-mediated creep.
Tungsten-interlayer samples will exhibit a change in creep activation energy associated with the mechanism transition.
Tungsten-interlayer samples will exhibit a change in strain-rate behavior associated with the mechanism transition.
TEM will reveal emergent dislocation structures at or near the tungsten interface.
HEA multilayers without tungsten interlayers are dominated by diffusion-mediated creep at lower temperatures.
The effectiveness of tungsten in producing the transition depends on tungsten-layer thickness.
The effectiveness of tungsten in producing the transition depends on the degree of interfacial coherency.
The effectiveness of tungsten in producing the transition depends on the applied temperature and stress window.
Very thick or incoherent tungsten layers might not produce the proposed creep-mechanism transition.
